sm: Host Kate Del opens this Thanksgiving-eve Potomac Watch with columnists Matt Cottonetti and Joe Sternberg, looking at the early 2028 Democratic primary. Matt says the race is wide open. The polling average has Kamala Harris at sixteen and a half percent, Jon Ossoff at fifteen, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Pete Buttigieg at fourteen each, and Gavin Newsom at eleven. He argues that after the big midterm win, Democratic voters want new faces, which helps Ossoff and Ocasio-Cortez and hurts Harris, Buttigieg and Newsom. Kate notes Buttigieg's record as transportation secretary may draw scrutiny. They then turn to the Democratic National Committee's plan for twelve primary debates, with chair Ken Martin calling it a strenuous test for candidates.

Joe says he isn't opposed to many debates, since they expose candidates' views, but he warns it depends on the questions. He fears Democrats will face questions on transgender health care for prisoners, exotic abortion scenarios and off-putting foreign policy topics that could hurt them in a general election. The discussion then moves to Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro's interview with the Journal, in which he tries to be an adult on national security, tough on Russia and critical of how Biden and Trump handled Netanyahu. Matt says that lane exists and is basically the Democratic mainstream on foreign policy. He adds that the most notable part of Martin's announcement was the demand that candidates swear off PACs to take part in debates, which is aimed at AIPAC and complicates the use of super PACs.

Matt says Shapiro isn't in the polls yet but has a path to the nomination, and that showing toughness on Israel matters given his Jewish identity. He expects governors like Shapiro, Wes Moore, J.B. Pritzker, Newsom, Mikie Sherrill and possibly Abigail Spanberger to pitch themselves as people who get things done. Kate says Democratic hawks are an endangered species, citing Ro Khanna's call for war reparations checks over Iran. Matt says Shapiro's focus on Netanyahu works only while Netanyahu leads Israel, and that most Democratic candidates say they want the Iran war to end without saying how. Joe then says the big coming fights are economic policy, such as Medicare for All messaging, and entitlement reform. He worries about a deal with Trump on Social Security, where the trust fund runs out in 2032, possibly through a large payroll tax increase.

Joe says Democrats must also guess what the Republican side will look like, noting Shapiro tied Marco Rubio and J.D. Vance to the Trump administration. Kate asks whether Democrats assume Vance will be the Republican nominee. Matt says Democrats mostly plan to run against Trump, who will dominate the next two years and whose shadow will fall on any Republican nominee. He finds it unlikely the party picks someone outside the administration, though Rubio is ahead of Vance in some polls. He recalls past vice presidents like George H. W. Bush and Al Gore who faced doubts before winning nominations. Joe adds that Trump's views fit awkwardly with the old Republican mainstream, so Republicans may find it easier to distance themselves from him, and Democrats shouldn't assume running against Trump will be enough.
